# Introduction 

This course covers agentic coding workflows specializing in geospatial data science. You will get hands-on experience setting up your agent and understand how to use skills and MCP servers to augment domain-specific capabilities. We cover best practices for using coding agents to rapidly solve complex problems - grounded in established science and human-in-the-loop validation. We cover hands-on examples using Claude Code - including crime hotspot mapping, route optimization, and object detection from aerial imagery. You will also learn how to use agents to manage a personal knowledge base and create a website that automatically updates with new information.

[![View Presentation](images/agentic_coding_geospatial/introduction.png){width="400px"}](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1gQV_YIBTE_o8ziY0Oza-BX8BOmvATfPq6vHaC4_cNKI/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}

[Google Slides &#8599;](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1gQV_YIBTE_o8ziY0Oza-BX8BOmvATfPq6vHaC4_cNKI/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"} [PDF &#8599;](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/presentations/Agentic_Coding_for_Geospatial_Introduction.pdf){target="_blank"}

# Get the Course Videos

The videos for this course are currently being edited. We expect them to be available by end of November 2026.

# Get the Data Package

The code examples and reference materials used in this course are supplied to you in the `agentic_coding_geospatial.zip` file. Unzip this file to a directory - preferably to the `<home folder>/Desktop/agentic_coding_geospatial/` folder. 

Download [agentic_coding_geospatial.zip](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/data/agentic_coding_geospatial.zip){target="_blank"}.

> Note: Certification and Support are only available for participants in our paid instructor-led classes.

# Installation and Preparation

## Sign up for GitHub

Visit [GitHub.com](https://github.com/){target="_blank"} and create a free account. If you already have an account, skip this step.

## Install Git and GitHub CLI

Follow our [Git and GitHub CLI Installation Guide](install-git-github.html){target="_blank"} to install and configure Git and GitHub CLI.

## Install Conda and Set up an Environment

We will use conda to install the required Python packages and manage local development environments. 

Follow our step-by-step [Conda Installation Guide](install-conda.html){target="_blank"} to install Miniconda for your operating system. Once you have a working conda installation, follow the steps below.

1. *(Windows users)*: Search for Anaconda Powershell Prompt and launch it. *(Mac/Linux users)*: Launch a Terminal window. Run the following commands to create a fresh environment and activate it.

```{bash eval=FALSE}
conda create --name claude_code_workshop -y
conda activate claude_code_workshop
```

2. Now your environment is ready. We will install the required packages from `conda-forge`.

```{bash eval=FALSE}
conda install -c conda-forge pandas geopandas matplotlib jupyterlab rioxarray gdal rio-cogeo ipykernel uv
```

Your local development environment is now ready.

## Install Visual Studio Code

We recommend Visual Studio Code (VS Code) editor for this course. 

Follow our step-by-step [Visual Studio Code Installation Guide](install-vscode.html){target="_blank"} to install and configure VS Code on your system. Make sure to complete the steps to set VS Code as your default editor.

## Install Claude Code

Follow our step-by-step [Claude Code Installation Guide](install-claude-code.html){target="_blank"} to install and configure Claude Code on your system.

## Install Obsidian

[Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/){target="_blank"} is a free app for creating and managing notes. We will be using Obsidian for setting up your personal knowledge base using Claude. Visit [Obsidian Download](https://obsidian.md/download){target="_blank"} page and install Obsidian for your platform.

## Sign up for OpenRouteService API

[OpenRouteService (ORS)](https://openrouteservice.org/){target="_blank"} provides a free API for routing, distance matrix, geocoding, route optimization etc. using OpenStreetMap data. To obtain an API key, visit the [HeiGIT Sign Up page](https://account.heigit.org/signup){target="_blank"} and create an account. Once your account is activated, you can visit the [Dashboard](https://account.heigit.org/manage/key){target="_blank"} and copy the long string displayed under *Basic Key*. 

## Install QGIS

We will configure and use the QGIS MCP server to allow Claude Code to use QGIS directly. Please follow our [QGIS-LTR Installation Guide](install-qgis-ltr.html){target="_blank"} to install QGIS. If you already have a recent QGIS version (`3.40+` or `4.0+`) installed on your computer, you can skip this step.


# Get Familiar with the Terminal

Our primary interface for this course will be the Terminal. We will now cover basic terminal commands that will help you get comfortable with the environment.

*(Windows users)*: Search for Anaconda Powershell Prompt and launch it. *(Mac/Linux users)*: Launch a Terminal window. 

The following are some of the common terminal commands we will need to browse and manage files.


|   **Command**    | **Description**                     | **Example**     |
|:-----------------|:------------------------------------|:---------------------|
| `cd`             | Change directory                    | `cd Desktop` |
| `cd ..`          | Change to the parent directory      | `cd ..` |
| `ls`             | List files in the current directory | `ls` |
| `rm `            | Delete a file                       | `rm test.txt` |
| `rm -R`          | Delete a directory (Mac/Linux)      | `rm -R test` |
| `rm -Recurse`    | Delete a directory (Windows)        | `rm -Recurse test` |
| `mkdir`          | Create a directory                  | `mkdir test` |
| `cat`            | Print the contents of a file        | `cat test.txt` |
| `clear`          | Clear screen                        | `clear` |

## 1.1 Setting up your Agent

A good practice is to always set up a [CLAUDE.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory){target="_blank"} file for your project. This file contains instructions and rules to be followed when working inside the project directory. If you already have a directory with some code or have cloned a Git repository, Claude Code can automatically create the `CLAUDE.md` file using the `/init` command. Here we are starting with a blank project, so we will create a new `CLAUDE.md` file with instructions.

1. We will first navigate to the project directory and start Claude Code. *(Windows users)*: Search for Anaconda Powershell Prompt and launch it. *(Mac/Linux users)*: Launch a Terminal window. Use the `cd` command to change the current working directory to the project directory.

*Windows*

```{bash eval=FALSE}
cd Desktop\agentic_coding_geospatial
```

*Mac/Linux*

```{bash eval=FALSE}
cd Desktop/agentic_coding_geospatial
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init1.png')
```

2. Once you are inside the project folder, launch Claude Code by entering the following command. The first time you start Claude Code inside a directory, there will be a security notification. You can choose **Yes, I trust this folder**. 

```{bash eval=FALSE}
claude
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init2.png')
```

3. Invoke the `/memory` command to set up the project `CLAUDE.md`

```
/memory
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init3.png')
```

4. Select **Project instructions** and press *Enter*.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init4.png')
```

5. Your default editor (Visual Studio Code) will now open with a new `CLAUDE.md` file. Paste the following content and save the file. Close the file once saved.

```
# CLAUDE.md

## Geospatial Stack Preferences

- Prefer Python-based approaches
- Use existing packages instead of building solutions from scratch
- My preference for geospatial packages are below
  - Pandas for tabular data
  - GeoPandas for vector geospatial data
  - XArray ecosystem (rioxarray, xarray-spatial etc) for raster geospatial data
  - Scikit-learn for Machine Learning
  - GeoAI (geoai-py) for Deep Learning
  - Matplotlib/Folium/Lonboard for data visualization in notebooks

## Other Preferences

- Write code that is simple to understand and explain
- Always install python packages in a conda environment. Never install anything in the base environment. Ask the user for confirmation on their preferred conda environment before installing anything.
- Do not use emojis
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init5.png')
```

6. Make sure you now have a `CLAUDE.md` file in your `<home folder>/Desktop/agentic_coding_geospatial/` folder.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init6.png')
```

7. You can also use the `/context` command to check if the file contents have been loaded into the current context. 

> Note: Learn more about [Managing Context](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices#manage-context-aggressively){target="_blank"}

```
/context
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init7.png')
```

8. Verify that you have the Memory file in the context.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/init8.png')
```

9. At the prompt, you can invoke several [commands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands){target="_blank"} for configuration. You can type `/help` to see all available commands. Let's run a few commands. First enable [Plan mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#analyze-before-you-edit-with-plan-mode){target="_blank"} by entering the `/plan` command. Next choose the model using the `/model` command. The default model choice is good for now, and you can change the model at any time.


# 2. Geospatial Data Analysis (Mapping Crime Hotspots)

We will now use Claude Code to do some data exploration, cleaning and analysis. This will give you a feel of how agents work and how to guide them. We will take the Police.uk data on street-level crime for the City of London (The *Square Mile* area) and identify crime hotspots.

## 2.1 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

1. Enter the following prompt into Claude Code and press *Enter*. Make sure the *Plan mode* is on. This will ensure Claude Code will first make an implementation plan and wait for your approval before diving into coding.

```
I would like to do an exploratory data analysis of crime data in the folder data/london_crime_2024. 

* Give me a summary of the rows, columns and any missing data. 
* Flag any data quality issues. 
* Create charts showing different types of crime and monthly patterns.

Produce the output as a Python script and PNG images.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda1.png')
```

2. As the project-level `CLAUDE.md` states, all the work needs to be done in a conda virtual environment. Claude Code will prompt you to choose an environment. Choose the **claude_code_workshop** environment created for this class and press *Enter*.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda2.png')
```

3. For the *Output format*, choose **Python script + saved PNGs**.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda3.png')
```

4. Review the answers and select *Submit answers*. Press *Enter*.

> Note: Depending on your operating system, Claude Code version, and selected model, you may see a slightly different set of questions.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda4.png')
```

5. Now Claude Code will go through the data and come up with a plan for building the required script for exploratory data analysis. You can review the plan and edit it as per your requirements. Use the *Ctrl+G* shortcut to open an editor with the plan and make any necessary edits. Once you are satisfied, confirm the execution by selecting **Yes, and use auto mode**.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda5.png')
```

6. Claude Code will write the Python script and run it using the installed packages in the conda environment.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda6.png')
```

7. Once done, it will print the summary of its findings.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/eda7.png')
```

8. The analysis will also produce some charts in the `outputs/` subfolder.
 

Now that we have a good understanding of the data structure, we can ask Claude Code to help us with analyzing the data. In this section, we will go through the workflow of identifying theft hotspots. 1. Back in Claude Code, switch to *Plan mode*. You can press *Shift+Tab* until you see *plan mode on*. Enter the following prompt. Claude Code will ask you clarifying questions. You can read through the explanation and select the options that make sense for the analysis.

```
I want to analyze theft hotspots. 
Help me select the categories for theft crimes and filter the data.
```

3. Select *Submit answers* and press *Enter*.


# 3. Using Web APIs (Route Optimization)

In this section, we will learn how to use Claude Code to build Jupyter notebooks for data analysis and interactively guide the agent to reach the desired solution and validate the results. We will be implementing a real-world scenario of optimizing delivery routes based on a route optimization algorithm.

In your data package, you will find the following files in the `data/route_optimization/` folder.

* `Delivery_Locations.geojson`: A set of 100 addresses in Washington DC area representing delivery locations.
* `Grocery_Store_Locations.geojson`: A set of 14 grocery store locations which need to fulfill the delivery to these locations.

We will use Claude Code to build a Jupyter Notebook that builds an end-to-end workflow that loads the data, finds optimal delivery routes and writes PDF manifests with delivery schedule for each store.


[![View Presentation](images/agentic_coding_geospatial/optimization.png){width="400px"}](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1qF0D-697kSUbosBGBZkNYfQ7sn4pxcvGI53OpWs9dGE/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}

[Google Slides &#8599;](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1qF0D-697kSUbosBGBZkNYfQ7sn4pxcvGI53OpWs9dGE/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"} [PDF &#8599;](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/presentations/Agentic_Coding_for_Geospatial_Network_Analysis_and_Route_Optimization.pdf){target="_blank"}

## 3.3 Interactive Data Analysis

Now, let's build the core of our data analysis to find the optimal delivery routes. This is a complex problem that requires a lot more context and direction. We will use the *Plan mode* and guide Claude Code towards building the code that solves the problem.

1. Make sure the notebook `route_optimization.ipynb` is open. Open Claude Code from the *Toggle Chat* button.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/interactive1.png')
```

2. Switch to *Plan mode*.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/interactive2.png')
```

3. Enter the following prompt.

```
I want to use OpenRouteService API. 
Give me options on different approaches to plan for the most optimal delivery routes from each store. 

Here are the constraints:

- A single trip will consist of 10 deliveries at maximum.
- The delivery will originate at a grocery store and end at the same delivery store.
- All stores are capable of fulfilling the order but can do a maximum of 5 delivery trips each day.

The goal is to minimize the total distance traveled.

The output is the assignment and delivery schedule for each store along with a GeoJSON of the optimal delivery routes for visual inspection.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/interactive3.png')
```

4. Claude Code will trigger the *AskUserQuestion* tool to collect more information. For the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) approach, select the **ORS Optimization API (VROOM)**.

# Assignment

Now you are ready to put your agentic coding skills to test by solving a spatial analysis problem from scratch. 

**Problem Statement**

You are a data scientist for a real-estate company who wants to enhance their property listings by assigning a **livability score** to each of their properties to help buyers pick properties that suit their lifestyle. 

Your task is to calculate such a score for all the *Apartment Buildings* in your city. Consider the factors that are important to home buyers. You can design the score using metrics such as:

* Total number of parks within a certain distance
* Total number of restaurants within a certain distance
* Distance to the nearest metro/rail/bus stop
* Distance to the nearest school
* ...

These are some examples and you can pick the criteria that make sense to you based on the knowledge of your city. You can use OpenStreetMap to obtain the data for apartment building polygons and the required amenities.

**Required output**

* A GeoPackage containing the apartment buildings layer enriched with attributes for each factor and the final livability score.
* A 1-2 page report on your analysis describing the methodology and steps you have taken to validate the results. 

Below are example reports shared by participants of our live class for inspiration:

* [Livability of Stockholm's apartment buildings](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/documents/stockholm_livability_report.pdf){target="_blank"} by Marco Hernández
* [Bozeman Apartment Livability Index: Methodology Report](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/documents/Bozeman_Livability_Index_Methodology_Report.pdf){target="_blank"} by Colin A. Shaw

**Tips**

* You can prompt the agent to use the Python package `osmnx` which can easily extract the required data from OpenStreetMap.
* Instead of trying to one-shot the whole analysis, build your notebook by prompting the agent to plan and build one step at a time. Validate the output from each step before moving to the next.
* Start simply and use a simple buffer / linear distance. You may add an option to use a network distance or isochrone instead of a simple circular buffer for more realistic distances.
* Look at methodology followed by existing livability scores on websites such as [AreaVibes](https://www.areavibes.com/madison-wi/capitol/){target="_blank"} and [PropTiger](https://www.proptiger.com/buzz/livability-score){target="_blank"}.


# 4. Using Skills

Skills are a set of instructions that teach an AI agent how to perform specific, multi-step workflows. [Skills in Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills){target="_blank"} are defined by a `SKILL.md` containing natural-language instructions for the agent along with specific examples and patterns. You can also publish your skill on GitHub and make it available for others to download and use with their own agent.

[![View Presentation](images/agentic_coding_geospatial/skills.png){width="400px"}](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/18zyVBK70rY-mv0tiZwKQqRO6pY1A4762HAYrJCVKCjk/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}

[Google Slides &#8599;](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/18zyVBK70rY-mv0tiZwKQqRO6pY1A4762HAYrJCVKCjk/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"} [PDF &#8599;](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/presentations/Agentic_Coding_for_Geospatial_Using_Skills.pdf){target="_blank"}


## 4.1 Installing a Skill

We will install the [Humanizer](https://github.com/blader/humanizer/tree/main){target="_blank"} skill that improves the text generated by AI models and makes them sound more natural.

1. Start Claude Code in the Terminal. *(Windows users)*: Search for Anaconda Powershell Prompt and launch it. *(Mac/Linux users)*: Launch a Terminal window. Use the `cd` command to change the current working directory to the project directory. Once you are inside the project folder, launch Claude Code by entering the following command.

```{bash eval=FALSE}
claude
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/installskill1.png')
```

2. There are multiple ways to install skills. The [`npx skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills){target="_blank"} command provides an easy way to install skills for a wide range of coding agents. However this requires installation of Node.js on your system. For Claude Code, you can install skills as plugins. Run the following command to add the GitHub repository.

```
/plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/installskill2.png')
```

3. Next run the following command to install the `humanizer` skill as a plugin.

```
/plugin install humanizer@humanizer
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/installskill3.png')
```

4. When prompted, select **Install for you (user scope)**.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/installskill4.png')
```

5. The plugin will be installed and activated.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/installskill5.png')
```

## 4.4 Useful Skills

* [Anthropic Official Skills](https://github.com/anthropics/skills/tree/main){target="_blank"}: Official skills repository by Anthropic. `skill-creator`, `pdf`, `xlsx` are useful skills for Data Science work.
* [Karpathy-Inspired Claude Code Guidelines](https://github.com/multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills){target="_blank"}: Improve Claude Code behavior, derived from Andrej Karpathy's observations on LLM coding pitfalls.
* [Skills Leaderboard](https://www.skills.sh/){target="_blank"}: Discover, install and manage skills using the `skills` CLI.
* [Geospatial Skills for Agents](https://isaac.earth/geospatial-skills/#catalog){target="_blank"}: A catalog of installable geospatial tools and capabilities designed for coding agents, covering raster/vector processing, satellite data, and interactive visualization.
* [SpatialThoughts AI Skills](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/spatialthoughts-ai-skills/){target="_blank"}: Repository containing skills accompanied with Spatial Thoughts Courses. 
* [GeoSQL](https://github.com/dekart-xyz/geosql){target="_blank"}: Skill for data scientists and analysts working with geospatial data on PostGIS, BigQuery, Snowflake, and Wherobots.


# 5. Building a Personal Knowledge Website

An AI second brain is a persistent digital memory system that stores your notes and ideas. Andrej Karpathy popularized the idea of implementing such a knowledge base using the note taking app Obsidian and coding agents like Claude Code. In this section, we will take the core ideas behind the [LLM-Wiki](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f){target="_blank"} system and learn how to set up a simplified version to collect, organize and maintain an archive of your notes and bookmarks. We will also publish and host them as an auto-updating website on GitHub Pages so you can always find and recall items from your archive.

[![View Presentation](images/agentic_coding_geospatial/personal_knowledge.png){width="400px"}](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1w2N_7FtX4v9nHJoX-se3rLw-KcbfKepEhr9b6Lk7wPI/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}

[Google Slides &#8599;](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1w2N_7FtX4v9nHJoX-se3rLw-KcbfKepEhr9b6Lk7wPI/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"} [PDF &#8599;](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/presentations/Agentic_Coding_for_Geospatial_Personal_Knowledge_Base.pdf){target="_blank"}

# 6. Using MCP Servers (QGIS Multicriteria Overlay)

The [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/getting-started/intro){target="_blank"} is an open standard for connecting external tools to AI Agents. MCP Servers allow your Agent to carry out tasks on different applications. In this section, we will learn how MCP servers work and how to configure your agents to use them.

[![View Presentation](images/agentic_coding_geospatial/mcp.png){width="400px"}](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1uaxad3a4VE9AqHTUwyfiSqUIEch9kJeAzN6n27FlFj4/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}

[Google Slides &#8599;](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1uaxad3a4VE9AqHTUwyfiSqUIEch9kJeAzN6n27FlFj4/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"} [PDF &#8599;](https://github.com/spatialthoughts/courses/releases/download/presentations/Agentic_Coding_for_Geospatial_Using_MCP_Servers.pdf){target="_blank"}

## 6.1 Installing and Using the QGIS MCP Server

The QGIS MCP server allows you to connect Claude Code to QGIS and provides tools to add layers, edit features, call processing algorithms and more. Configuring the MCP server is a two-step process:

* Install the [QGIS MCP](https://plugins.qgis.org/plugins/qgis_mcp_plugin/){target="_blank"} plugin in QGIS. 
* Configure Claude Code with the QGIS MCP server.

We will go through each step and learn how to set up the server and use it from Claude Code.

1. Open QGIS. Go to **Plugins &rarr; Manage and Install Plugins...**.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp1.png')
```

2. In the *Plugin Manager*, select the *All* tab, search and locate the **QGIS MCP** plugin. Click on the *Install Plugin* button to install it.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp2.png')
```

3. Once installed, you may get a configuration pop-up. No need to change any settings here. Click *Close*.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp3.png')
```

4. Start the MCP server from **Plugins &rarr; QGIS MCP &rarr; Run MCP**.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp4.png')
```

5. You can also start the server from the *Plugin Toolbar* menu. Once started, the plugin button will turn green to indicate that the server is running.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp5.png')
```

6. *(Windows users)*: Search for Anaconda Powershell Prompt and launch it. *(Mac/Linux users)*: Launch a Terminal window. Activate the course environment and run the following command to add the QGIS MCP server to Claude Code configuration.

```{bash eval=FALSE}
conda activate claude_code_workshop
claude mcp add -s user qgis -- uvx --from https://github.com/nkarasiak/qgis-mcp/archive/refs/heads/main.zip qgis-mcp-server
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp6.png')
```

7. Start Claude Code. Run the following command for managing MCP servers.

```
/mcp
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp7.png')
```

8. Verify that `qgis` is connected. Press *Esc* to exit.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp8.png')
```

9. Enter the following prompt to test the connection to the QGIS MCP server. If the connection is working fine, you will get a success return message.

```
ping qgis
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp9.png')
```

10. Let's use the MCP server. Enter the following prompt.

```
Load the raster data/chirps/chirps-v3.0.2025.tif in QGIS
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp10.png')
```

11. Claude Code will use the tools provided by the MCP server to load the data layer in QGIS.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgismcp11.png')
```

## 6.2 Set up Project Instructions

Before we start asking our agent to perform tasks in QGIS, let's update our `CLAUDE.md` file with QGIS best practices and preferences.

1. Invoke the `/memory` command to update the project `CLAUDE.md`.

```
/memory
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgisinstructions1.png')
```

2. Select **Project instructions** and press *Enter*.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgisinstructions2.png')
```

3. Your default editor (Visual Studio Code) will now open with the project's `CLAUDE.md` file. Paste the following content after the first section. Save and close the file.

```
## QGIS Rules and Preferences

### Inputs and Outputs

- Never modify my input data sources and layers. Always create a new layer with your edits. 
- Create temporary memory layers for all intermediate outputs. 
- Always use GeoPackage as the format for saving the outputs, unless specified otherwise. 
  QGIS Projects can also be saved inside of a GeoPackage.

### Processing Algorithms

- Search the available algorithms and check if they can carry out the required tasks. 
  - If there are multiple algorithms, prefer the native QGIS algorithms.
- Always prefer built-in processing algorithms rather than writing your own.
  
### Spatial Index

- If you are running a processing algorithm that uses a spatial query or an overlay, check if the spatial index exists on the input layers, and if not, create one using the processing algorithm. `Create Spatial index`.
  - Check if the spatial index already exists first.
  - QGIS creates a spatial index for point layers automatically, so do this only for line and polygon layers. 
- When creating models, add the spatial index step to create a spatial index on intermediate layers where it is required.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/qgisinstructions3.png')
```


## 6.3 Spatial Analysis with QGIS MCP Server 

We will now use the QGIS MCP server to carry out a multicriteria overlay analysis. Our goal is to find suitable locations for new bicycle parking facilities based on several spatial criteria. We have a QGIS project with layers of bicycle theft hotspots, cycling routes, existing cycle parking and the borough boundary. We will ask Claude Code to design the workflow and run it in QGIS via the MCP Server.

1. Make sure QGIS is open and the MCP server is running. Enter the following prompt to load the project. Claude Code will open the `Bicycle_Theft_Multicriteria` project stored in the `multicriteria.gpkg` GeoPackage and summarize the layers it contains. 

```
Load the Bicycle_Theft_Multicriteria project from data/multicriteria_overlay/
in QGIS
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria1.png')
```

2. Switch to *Plan mode* (*Shift+Tab*) and enter the following prompt. We will ask Claude Code to suggest a workflow based on the layers we have, and will refine it to ensure it matches our expectation.

```
I want to do a multicriteria overlay analysis to find locations for new
bicycle parking facilities. Suggest the workflow to do this in QGIS with my
existing data layers.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria2.png')
```

3. Claude Code will propose a workflow. Once the plan is updated, press *Ctrl+G* to open it in Visual Studio Code and review it. 

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria3.png')
```

4. If you want to update the plan, close the file, and select **Tell Claude what to change** and enter what you want to change. For example, our initial plan excluded loading any intermediate layers and had questions about building a model. We can address these by entering the following prompt. Claude Code will update the plan. Press *Ctrl+G* to open it in Visual Studio Code and review it. When you are happy with the plan, save the file and close it.

```
Load all intermediate layers (turned off by default) so I can verify
the results. Also build a processing model with configurable distances.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria4.png')
```

5. Back in Claude Code, select **Yes, and use auto mode** to proceed.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria5.png')
```

6. Claude Code will run the analysis step by step using the MCP server, then run the new model with the same default distances and confirm both produce identical results. It will report the candidate zones ranked by the number of bicycle thefts inside each zone. In QGIS, you will see a `Results` group with the `candidate_zones` and `candidate_sites` layers. 

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria6.png')
```

7. Expand the `Intermediate` group and turn on the layers one at a time to verify the analysis. For example, turning on `01_routes_buffer`, `02_hotspots_buffer` and `03_parking_buffer` shows the areas near cycling routes, near theft hotspots and around existing parking. Checking the intermediate outputs visually is an important step in verifying the work done by an agent.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria7.png')
```

8. Turn off the `Intermediate` group and turn on the `candidate_sites` layer. Each point is a suggested site for new bicycle parking, located inside one of the candidate zones.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria8.png')
```

9. Once we have verified the results, we no longer need the intermediate layers. Read the *Things to know* section of the summary, which notes small differences between the plan and the model, such as the output names. Enter the following prompt to clean up the project.

```
Remove the intermediate layers from the QGIS project.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria9.png')
```

10. The model created by Claude Code is a regular QGIS processing model that anyone can run without an agent. In the *Browser* panel, expand the `multicriteria_overlay` folder and double-click the `Bicycle Parking Site Selection` model to open it. The *Parameters* tab shows all the inputs we can configure. Let's see what happens if we change one of them. Set *Buffer around theft hotspots (m)* to **0**, *Min distance from existing parking* to **50** and *Max distance from cycling route* to **50**. Click *Run*.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria10.png')
```

11. A new set of `candidate_sites` and `candidate_zones` layers will be added to the project. Compare the new sites with the original ones. Changing the parameters resulted in a very different output. The results of a multicriteria overlay depend on the distance thresholds we pick, and these thresholds are often a judgement call. In the next section, we will test how sensitive our results are to these choices.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/multicriteria11.png')
```

## 6.4 Sensitivity Analysis with QGIS Models

A sensitivity analysis tests how the results change when the input parameters change. Sites that are selected across a wide range of buffer values are reliable choices, while sites that appear only for certain values depend on our assumptions. Since we have a processing model with configurable distances, we can ask Claude Code to run it many times with different values and summarize the results.

1. Enter the following prompt.

```
I want to do sensitivity analysis to test for the effects of different buffer
values. Use the QGIS model to run different variables of the analysis to
reliably detect candidate sites.
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/sensitivity1.png')
```

2. Claude Code will describe its design before running the model. In this instance it decided to run the model 27 times, covering every combination of 3 values each for `route_distance`, `hotspot_buffer` and `parking_distance`, while keeping `min_area` fixed at 500 m2. It then counted how often each location falls in a candidate zone, using a 25 m point grid over Westminster. This gives the share of runs in which each location is selected.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/sensitivity2.png')
```

3. Once the runs are complete, Claude Code will report how often each of the original candidate sites was selected. Sites 4 and 2 were selected in all 27 runs and are marked as *Robust*. The other sites appear only for certain combinations of buffer values. Scroll down to read how each buffer affects the results.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/sensitivity3.png')
```

4. In QGIS, you will see a `Sensitivity results` group. The `site_stability` layer shows each candidate site styled by the percentage of runs in which it was selected. Turn on only the **82.4 - 100** category to see the 2 sites that are selected regardless of the buffer values. These are the most reliable locations for new bicycle parking. The group also contains a `robustness_grid` layer with the selection frequency for each grid point, a `robust_zones_75pct` layer with areas selected in at least 75% of the runs, and a `run_summary` table with the results of each run.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('images/agentic_coding_geospatial/sensitivity4.png')
```

## 7.3 Using Deep Learning Models

With the Colab MCP server connected, we can now ask Claude Code to build a complete deep learning workflow. We will use a pre-trained building footprint extraction model from the GeoAI package, run it on a free GPU in Colab and verify the detected buildings against the source imagery.

1. Enter the following prompt to build the notebook.

```
Create a new Colab notebook named "building_detection".

This notebook will use a pre-trained model for building footprint extraction from GeoAI and run it on the provided image. 

Structure the notebook following this example https://opengeoai.org/examples/building_footprints_africa/

The provided image can be large. So use the GeoAI package to split the input image into tiles 

Reproject the tiles to a suitable local UTM crs.

The model is trained on images around 50cm-1m resolution images. Check the resolution of the provided image and if it is higher resolution (i.e. 5cm, 10cm) - resample the tiles to 50cm resolution before running the inference. 

Save the results as a GeoJSON file in EPSG:4326 CRS.
```

## Exercise

You will notice that since the footprints were vectorized from a raster layer, they have jagged edges. We can make the output polygons much better by *Regularizing* the polygons. GeoAI has several algorithms for [Building Regularization](https://opengeoai.org/examples/building_regularization/){target="_blank"}. Prompt Claude Code to add a step at the end to regularize the polygons and save them.
